## Hands-on 5 – The preregistration {#the-preregistration-moment .smaller}

::: {.big}
- Aim 2: assess the **robustness** of the constrained result
:::

::: {.none}
1. Open the preregistration block in your report
2. Complete fields 1–5: the claim, the data-in-hand statement, your one specification, the one-sentence justification from your DAG, and your rule for what supports or undermines the claim
3. Run the block, then **render** the report; in the slides, copy the completed cell into your notes
4. Only then run your specification, on the slides that follow
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the workspace:** the chunk `prereg` of `index.qmd`, which ends with the call `prereg()`.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Nothing runs until your block is complete.
:::

::: notes
Your second aim as the sixth analyst is to assess the robustness of the constrained result. In Task 4 you explored, trying specifications in whatever order took your interest, which was the right way to learn them; now you preregister one, and the code is identical, the difference being that an exploratory specification can be chosen because of its result and a preregistered one cannot. Open the preregistration block of your report. Fill in the five fields: the claim, the data-in-hand statement, your one specification with an option for each of the fourteen decisions, the one-sentence justification that your graph gives you, and the rule – written now, before any result – for what would support the claim and what would undermine it. The data-in-hand statement is where you record what you already know about the data before you fix your specification. Render the report; the rendered file with its timestamp is the dated record of your preregistration, like the frozen snapshot that the OSF keeps of a registration. If you work in the slides, copy the completed cell into your notes. You run nothing before that record exists. And if the specification you choose is one that you already tried in Task 4, that is allowed, but say so in the block, because a specification whose result you have already seen is not preregistered in the strict sense.
:::

## Hands-on 5 – The preregistration cell {#hands-on-5-the-preregistration-cell .smaller}

::: {.small}
One choice on each of the fourteen decisions, in the three groups of the menu; an option that is off the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the workshop convention.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the workspace:** the chunk `prereg` of `index.qmd`, the same block.
:::

::: {.fs-70}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| max-lines: 15
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: europeanisation_cy.csv (270 country-years,
#    public); I know that the reproduced specification gives t = -3.804,
#    and what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 864 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# The question (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome      <- "mcosmo"       # mcosmo | mutil | mpos   (the positive framings)
my_predictor    <- "unemp"        # unemp | growth    (the measure whose coefficient tests the claim)
my_copredictor  <- "none"         # none | other      (the other economic measure, adjusted for)
my_estimator    <- "fe_twoway"    # fe_twoway | fe_country
my_sample       <- "all"          # all    (the 27 member states, 2004–2013)
my_weights      <- "none"         # none   (every country-year counts once)
my_construction <- "share"        # share  (the share of a respondent's own mentions)

# Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_noop         <- "zero"         # zero | drop   (respondents who mentioned no frame at all)
my_item_set     <- "all"          # all | un   (with or without the "unemployment" item)
my_cell_weight  <- "unweighted"   # unweighted | design   (cells as interviewed, or weighted)
my_measure      <- "wb_nat"       # unemp:  wb_nat | es_1574_act | es_2064_pop | es_2564_lfs
                                  # growth: wb_growth

# The model (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_pred_form    <- "raw"          # raw | log   (growth: raw only; centring or z-scaling
                                  #              would leave t, r and p unchanged)
my_family       <- "gaussian"     # gaussian   (a linear model of the cell means)
my_se           <- "cr2"          # cr2   (fixed: CR2 errors clustered by country)

claim_align     <- TRUE           # the workshop convention, applied automatically

# 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: .......................
# 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative with CR2
#    p < .05; undermined if it is not significant or positive. I will
#    report what I get.
```
:::

::: notes
This is the block, the same in the slides as in your report. The numbered comments map onto the questions of the short AsPredicted template, and field two also stands in for the section on prior knowledge of the template for secondary data, a section that AsPredicted leaves out. In the middle sit the fourteen decisions in their three groups: seven about the question, four about measurement and three about the model. The curve keeps two or more options on nine of them, and a single option on the other five, the sample, the weighting, the scoring rule, the model family and the inference. [scroll through the cell] Change the lines of the decisions that you declare, fill the dotted lines of fields one and four, and run the cell. It prints nothing: it fixes your choices for the rest of the session, and every later cell reads the choices from here.
:::

## Hands-on 5 – The declaration {#hands-on-5-the-declaration .smaller}

::: {.small}
`prereg()` checks every choice against the menu and prints the preregistration. In the slides, the completed cell, copied into your notes, is the record of the declaration.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the workspace:** the last line of the chunk `prereg` of `index.qmd`.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
prereg()
```

::: notes
Then prereg reads the fourteen choices from the block, checks each against the menu, and prints the declaration in its three groups, with the convention of claim alignment at the end. [run it] An option that is off the curve stops it here, with the reason why and the page of the workshop that teaches it, as try underscore spec did in Task 4. In your report the call sits at the end of the same chunk, so a render prints the declaration under the block, with the date of the render. An optional mirror form collects the preregistrations of the class, and its link is on the screen, but the block itself is the record.
:::

## Hands-on 5 – The preregistered run {#run-it-then-watch-the-chart .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Task 5** – translate the declaration into model syntax yourself, and run that specification and only that one
- `build_model()` accepts only the outcome, the predictor terms and the estimator code that you declared, and its errors say what is off
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the workspace:** the chunk `build-model` of `index.qmd`.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_model <- build_model(______ ~ ______, estimator = "______")
```

::: {.fragment .fs-80}
The formula uses the columns of `europeanisation`: `mcosmo ~ unemp` for the reproduced specification, `mcosmo ~ log(unemp)` with the log form, `mcosmo ~ unemp + growth` with a co-predictor. The estimator is the menu code in quotes, `"fe_twoway"` or `"fe_country"`.
:::

::: notes
Go. Run the specification in your preregistration, just that one, and first translate it into model syntax yourself. The cell has three gaps, the outcome, the right-hand side and the estimator code, all as you declared them. build underscore model reads your declaration and accepts nothing else, and its error messages tell you what is off. Write the log form as log of unemp, and add any co-predictor with a plus. [advance] You do not write the fixed-effects syntax here, because the estimator code stands for it, and the cells of C6HJR and KQXUE in Task 3 showed what it expands to. Apart from the log form, the measurement decisions and the decisions about the model never appear in the formula: they select which version of the panel the result comes from. In your report the chunk build-model holds the same call.
:::

## Hands-on 5 – The run and the report {#hands-on-5-the-run-and-the-report .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
`run_spec()` prints the declared specification with the lines of Task 4; `report_result()` prints the link to the form, and your dot joins the **Class results** page as a *declared* result.\
**In the workspace:** the chunks `run-spec` and `report` of `index.qmd`.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_model)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

::: notes
When the model is accepted, run it. [run it] run underscore spec prints the same lines as in Task 4, and the placement is the share of the curve that lies further in the direction of the claim than yours. In the slides the result is read from the curve; in your workspace run underscore spec fits the model and computes its CR2 test on your machine, and the numbers are the same. Then report underscore result prints a link to the Google Form with your values already filled in, one click and you have submitted, and your dot joins the chart as a declared result, beside the exploratory dots of Task 4. Compare the two waves: if the preregistered dots fall systematically to one side of the exploratory ones, that is worth a conversation. If anything misbehaves, raise your hand and work down the ladder on the cheatsheet; as a last resort your specification is one row of the curve, which the download button on the Specification curve page serves, and I will help you submit it by hand.
:::
